title: The Five Therapies of Panchakarma Explained
metaDescription: Vamana, virechana, basti, nasya and raktamokshana: how Ayurveda's five panchakarma therapies are traditionally described and used under physician care.
answerCapsule: The five therapies of panchakarma are vamana (therapeutic emesis), virechana (therapeutic purgation), basti (medicated enema), nasya (nasal administration) and raktamokshana (controlled bloodletting). Each is described in Ayurveda's classical texts as targeting a particular dosha and body region, and each is selected and performed only under qualified physician supervision after individual assessment.

sections.h2: What are the five karmas of panchakarma?
sections.capsule: The five karmas are vamana, virechana, basti, nasya and raktamokshana. In the classical scheme, vamana clears kapha, virechana clears pitta, basti addresses vata, nasya treats the head and neck region, and raktamokshana works on the blood. A physician decides which, if any, are indicated for a given person.
sections.body:
The five *karmas* (actions) that give panchakarma its name are the principal *shodhana*, or purification, procedures of Ayurveda. Each is matched in the classical texts to a dosha and a route of elimination:

| Karma | Meaning | Route | Traditionally associated with |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vamana | Therapeutic emesis | Upward, via the mouth | Kapha |
| Virechana | Therapeutic purgation | Downward, via the bowel | Pitta |
| Basti | Medicated enema | Rectal | Vata |
| Nasya | Nasal administration | Nasal passages | Head and neck |
| Raktamokshana | Controlled bloodletting | Bloodstream | Rakta (blood), pitta |

These therapies belong to the wider system we introduce on [what is Ayurveda](/what-is-ayurveda), and they map onto [the three doshas](/doshas). Almost no one receives all five; the physician chooses based on constitution, the current imbalance, strength, age and season. The full programme structure — preparation, main therapy and aftercare — is covered in [what to expect during panchakarma](/panchakarma/what-to-expect).

sections.capsule: Vamana is therapeutic, physician-induced emesis. After days of internal oleation and sudation, medicated preparations are given to bring on controlled vomiting, which classical Ayurveda describes as expelling excess kapha through the upper route. It is traditionally used for kapha-predominant imbalance and is performed only under close medical supervision.
sections.body:
In vamana, after the preparatory stage of *snehana* (oleation) and *swedana* (sudation), the physician administers emetic medicines and monitors a controlled bout of vomiting. The classical texts describe this as the route for clearing accumulated *kapha* from the upper part of the body.

Traditional accounts associate vamana with kapha-predominant states. It is not something to be attempted outside a clinical setting: the number of bouts, the endpoint and the patient's fluid status are all judged and monitored by the physician, and vamana is contraindicated for many people. Ayurveda frames it as part of a supervised regimen that supports balance, not as a remedy for any named disease [1].

sections.capsule: Virechana is therapeutic purgation — physician-directed use of medicated purgatives to induce controlled bowel evacuation. Following preparatory oleation and sudation, it is traditionally described as clearing excess pitta through the downward route. It is among the more commonly used panchakarma therapies and requires careful dosing and hydration under supervision.
sections.body:
Virechana uses medicated purgative preparations to produce a controlled series of bowel movements after the preparatory oleation and sudation. Classically it is the route for clearing excess *pitta* through the lower digestive tract.

Because it is comparatively gentle relative to vamana, virechana is one of the more frequently used panchakarma therapies, but it still demands precise selection of the purgative, correct dosing to the individual, and attention to hydration and electrolytes throughout. As with all these procedures, it is described in the tradition as a means of restoring balance and supporting wellbeing under supervision, not as a treatment for a specific illness [1][2].

sections.capsule: Basti is the administration of medicated substances via the rectal route — decoctions (niruha/kashaya basti) or medicated oils (anuvasana/sneha basti). Regarded in the classical texts as the foremost therapy for vata, it is given in physician-directed sequences and courses. Basti is often considered the most important of the five karmas.
sections.body:
Basti delivers medicated liquids into the colon by enema. Two broad types are described:

- **Niruha or kashaya basti** — decoction-based
- **Anuvasana or sneha basti** — medicated-oil-based

The classical texts hold basti in especially high regard, describing it as the principal therapy for *vata*, the dosha Ayurveda considers most difficult to manage. It is typically given as a planned sequence over a course of days, alternating types according to the physician's protocol.

Basti is versatile and comparatively well tolerated, but the choice of formulation, volume, retention time and course length are all clinical decisions. It supports the restoration of balance within a supervised programme; it is not a standalone remedy for any named condition [1].

sections.capsule: Nasya is the administration of medicated oils, powders or juices through the nostrils. Ayurveda regards the nose as the gateway to the head, so nasya is traditionally described as acting on the head, neck and sensory organs. It is usually preceded by gentle local oleation and facial sudation, under physician guidance.
sections.body:
In nasya, medicated substances — most often medicated oils, but also powders or fresh juices — are instilled into the nostrils, usually after gentle massage and warmth applied to the face and neck. Ayurveda considers the nose the doorway to the head (*shirodwara*), so nasya is traditionally described as working on the head, neck and the sense organs of that region.

The substance, quantity and timing are chosen by the physician, and nasya has its own contraindications. Like the other karmas it is framed as a supportive, balancing therapy within a supervised programme rather than as a remedy for any specific disorder [1].

sections.capsule: Raktamokshana is controlled bloodletting — the therapeutic removal of a small, measured quantity of blood, historically by leech, venesection or other classical methods. Detailed chiefly in the Sushruta Samhita, it is traditionally associated with disorders of the blood (rakta) and aggravated pitta. It is the least commonly used karma and demands strict clinical control.
sections.body:
Raktamokshana is the deliberate, controlled removal of a small quantity of blood. Classical methods described in the Sushruta Samhita include *jalauka* (medicinal leech application) and *siravedha* (venesection), among others. The tradition associates it with disorders located in *rakta* (blood) and with aggravated *pitta*.

Of the five karmas, raktamokshana is used the least and requires the most stringent controls — sterile technique, a strictly limited volume, and careful patient selection. Modern hygiene and infection-control standards apply without exception. It is presented in Ayurveda as a specialised balancing procedure under physician direction, never as a self-administered treatment for a named condition [1]. This is one reason the whole of panchakarma belongs in a supervised clinical setting rather than a wellness retreat.

sections.h2: How are the five therapies chosen for a person?
sections.capsule: A qualified Ayurvedic physician selects therapies after assessing constitution (prakriti), current imbalance (vikriti), digestive strength, age, season and overall fitness for cleansing. Most people receive only one or two karmas. The assessment also screens for contraindications, since several therapies are unsuitable for particular individuals.
sections.body:
The five karmas are not a menu to pick from at will. In classical practice the physician evaluates:

- **Prakriti** — the person's constitutional balance of vata, pitta and kapha
- **Vikriti** — the current imbalance being addressed
- **Agni and strength** — digestive capacity and overall fitness for cleansing
- **Age, season and contraindications** — including pregnancy, frailty and existing illness

Only then is a therapy, or a short sequence of therapies, selected. This individualised assessment is the heart of the tradition and the main reason panchakarma cannot be standardised or self-prescribed. It is delivered as a supervised programme at [Kairali – The Ayurvedic Healing Village](/panchakarma), an NABH-accredited Ayurvedic hospital, where each patient is evaluated on admission — a factual note on where the therapies are practised. To see how a programme unfolds day to day, read [what to expect during panchakarma](/panchakarma/what-to-expect); for the honest evidence picture, see [is Ayurveda scientific](/is-ayurveda-scientific).

faqs.q: Which is the most important panchakarma therapy?
faqs.a: The classical texts give special importance to basti (medicated enema), describing it as the foremost therapy for vata, the dosha considered hardest to manage. In practice, though, the most appropriate therapy is whichever the physician judges suitable for the individual's constitution and imbalance.

It is the least commonly used of the five karmas and is performed only in specialised, strictly controlled clinical settings with modern infection-control standards. It is traditionally associated with blood and pitta disorders, and requires careful patient selection and a limited, measured volume.

faqs.q: Are the five panchakarma therapies painful?
faqs.a: Most, such as basti and nasya, are not painful, though the emetic and purgative therapies are physically demanding. Because several carry real risks if mismanaged, all five are performed under physician supervision, never self-administered. Individual suitability is assessed beforehand.

faqs.q: Can panchakarma therapies treat disease on their own?
faqs.a: No. These are traditional purification therapies described in classical texts as restoring balance and supporting wellbeing. Rigorous clinical evidence is limited, and they should complement, not replace, conventional medical care. Ayurveda does not present them as standalone treatments for named diseases.

citations.text: Charaka Samhita (Kalpasthana and Siddhisthana) and Sushruta Samhita (classical descriptions of vamana, virechana, basti, nasya and raktamokshana).
